title.narrative: Food assistance to communities most affected by El Nino-induced drought

description.narrative: Mozambique is highly vulnerable to climate shocks which results in frequent droughts, floods, and cyclones. These events disproportionately affect vulnerable households including rural, rainfed-dependent agricultural communities. Increased drought frequency in Mozambique continues to drive humanitarian crises as communities experience reduced food production, income loss, and limited access to essential services.The 2023 El Niño event worsened Mozambique’s food insecurity. Disrupted rainfall and temperature patterns heavily impacted agriculture, with Ministry of Agriculture assessments revealing a 19% reduction in crop yields across 591,541 hectares, or a loss of 720,000 tons of cereals. Rising food prices further strain rural and urban households.In priority districts of Guro, Macossa, Tambara (Manica), and Maringue (Sofala), the drought affected over 189,000 people, including ~72,000 classified as IPC Phase 4 (Emergency), who required urgent assistance. These areas face compounded threats from drought and seasonal flooding due to their location in the Zambeze River basin. Poor harvests have led to displacements and coping strategies including migration to areas with better agricultural conditions and services.The 2024/2025 forecast anticipates normal to above-normal rainfall, potentially influenced by La Niña. Rain could improve agricultural prospects, but increases risks of flooding and storm damage, particularly in river basins. The likelihood of frequent storms underscores the urgent need for building climate resilience.The Government of Mozambique and partners have taken proactive steps, preparing a multi-sectoral drought appeal. This proposal highlights the urgency of adaptive actions to prevent deterioration and bolster resilience in Mozambique. Addressing immediate humanitarian needs while fostering climate adaptation will reduce vulnerability in the targeted affected communities.This CERF UFE contribution will enable WFP Mozambique to provide in-kind food assistance to 36,337 people most affected by the El Nino-induced drought for a period of three months. WFP will target the most vulnerable groups in the districts of Guro, Macossa, and Tambara in Manica province and Maringue district in Sofala province. These districts have been classified as IPC 4 and Drought Severity 1. The food basket will be composed of a monthly in-kind ration of cereals (10 kg/pers/month), pulses (2 kg/pers/month), oil (0.8 L/pers/month), and iodised salt (0.1 kg/pers/month), which represents 82% of an individual’s daily kcal requirements. The same beneficiaries will receive livelihood support from FAO to ensure that the livelihood support is used and not eaten / sold to meet basic food needs. WFP’s food assistance will be coordinated through the Food Security Cluster to avoid duplications with other partners assisting populations in the target districts. In addition, through the Climate Action envelope, WFP and FAO will promote climate-smart approaches by supporting around 1,600 smallholder farmers to be able to produce and conserve nutrient dense food throughout the year, through irrigation systems and cold storage, which are efficient and powered by solar energy. The selection of targeted communities and farmer groups will be conducted jointly by WFP and FAO. WFP and FAO will work in four districts in two provinces providing beneficiaries with production and post-harvest management techniques based on solar energy and local material. FAO will manage the irrigation-related component while WFP will lead the post-harvest management one. The type of low-cost technology to be provided will be selected based on specific local conditions that may vary from one target area to another. Both components include the provision of equipment and the delivery of relevant trainings. It is important to recognize that post-harvest management begins in the field before the crop maturity phase.
